introFa: کتاب «Open Veins of Latin America: Five Centuries of the Pillage of a Continent» نوشته Eduardo Galeano یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Open Veins of Latin America: Five Centuries of the Pillage of a Continent»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Pp. 781. The 1960s marked a watershed for the academic study of Latin America. The Cuban Revolution coincided with a growing preoccupation in the United States and Western Europe about the economic development of the so-called Third World. Government and Foundation funds promoted an expansion in graduate research which has finally borne fruit in a plentiful crop of monographs. This renewal of academic interest equally coincided with an intellectual movement in Latin America which sought an explanation for the economic and social backwardness of the continent in terms of its dependent role within the international system of Western Capitalism. The result has been a marked divergence in approach. Most of the research undertaken from the United States was characterized by a sub- merged positivism, with a heavy reliance on statistical and archival material only barely controlled by theorizing restricted to the middle range. By contrast the more ambitious advocates of the Dependency school, despite the paucity of available data, boldly encompassed within their scope all Latin American reality from the Spanish Conquest until the present day. Thus we have two distinct approaches, the one ultimately influenced by Comte or Weber, implicitly devoted to an objective view of knowledge and inclined to accept history as a progressive sequence of change, and the other increasingly moving via a reading of Lenin towards a Marxian notion of exploitation and final ' immiseration ', in which knowledge should be deployed to change reality. New Approaches to Latin American History is in effect a festschrift to Professor Lewis Hanke presented by a group of scholars, several now established in leading

The editors solicited essays dealing with problems rather than pieces of research material; hence the volume offers an excellent guide as to what its contributors consider significant for future debate. To my mind by far the most satisfying discussion deals with the social bases of political alignment in Columbia during the years 1840-60. Frank Safford vigorously disputes the view which holds that the civil strife of these years arose from an open conflict between landowners and a hard-pressed urban elite, a conflict at times expressed in regional terms between export and domestic sectors of the economy. Instead, Safford argues that members of the upper class frequently diversified their interests, investing in both land and trade. Recruitment to the Liberal and Conservative parties came from a relatively homogeneous elite, with the main difference between them consisting of an inherited proximity or distance from the chief institutions of power and prestige. In a significant aside he asserts that the term ' middle class ' is best applied to artisans and petty shopkeepers rather than to lawyers and merchants. All this I find persuasive. Doubts only arise when one considers the composition of the political constituency as distinct from the leadership of these parties. Where Safford seeks to destroy schematic categories, Richard Graham and Peter Smith unite to multiply them. In a discussion of the political power of the land- owning class, Graham rightly notes the common confusion in the use of the terms class and elite, but then by way of remedy advances the notion of interest groups whose demands rather mysteriously flow into what he calls the ' black box' of power. The ability to influence political decisions is the best test of the dominance of any particular group in society. Unfortunately, as Graham admits, the applica- tion of this criterion proves remarkably difficult, since without challenge or con- flict the exercise of power cannot be demonstrated. He concludes with a typology of landowners in politics, describing them variously as Armed, Contemptuous, Bargaining and Aldermanic. Following much the same line of interest, Peter Smith takes as his problem the prevalence of authoritarian regimes in Latin America, regimes at times openly dictatorial, at times masked by parliamentary institutions, which all nevertheless bear the marks of legitimate government. To meet the gap between this local reality and Max Weber's trilogy of the traditional, rational and charismatic forms of legitimacy, Smith invents the two further categories of Dominance and Achievement-expertise. The ability to seize and to hold power apparently confers its own warrant in Latin America. Similarly, rulers who can deliver the goods - peace or prosperity - are equally acceptable. It will be observed that neither author makes much of the State as an entity in its own right nor mentions its changing nature over the last century. In consequence their attempt to manufacture new categories of analysis appears to operate in an historical vacuum without much sense of temporal sequence or perception of the necessary connexion between changes in society and the prevailing order in politics. Elsewhere in this volume, Stuart Schwartz advocates prosopography as the basic instrument for research into the colonial elite, especially for office-holders. Granted the absence of open politics, the counting of heads may well prove the surest way of measuring the distribution of influence within colonial society. However, his essay, despite an impressive bibliography, partakes more of a call to arms than an actual engagement in debate. In general, throughout this collection one has a sense of strain. Most contributors have written a book and are now engaged in further research. But successful infantry commanders do not always make good staff officers. It is no surprise then to find here several excellent plans for tactical assaults on particular problem points, but not much in the way of a strategy for the main battle. If Latin Americans be any guide, anthropology suffers from much the same sort of theoretical deficiency as history. It consists of an historical survey of Indian culture and society before and after the Spanish Conquest, immediately followed by a description of the contemporary scene based almost exclusively upon a limited set of case-studies. By far the most incisive chapter deals with the progressive modifications in anthropological speculation brought about by a greater concentra- tion upon the economic bases of society. Well aware of the peculiarly limited range of data employed within his discipline, Michael Olien calls for the elaboration of an ethno-history to bridge the chasm which lies between our knowledge of people in the sixteenth century and the present day, and in addition demands an overall analysis of modern society to provide a context for local case-studies. Whether anthropology would survive such a drastic expansion in scope remains to be seen. In the absence of any recent synthesis incorporating the field work of the last decade, the writers of text-books inevitably are driven back upon the same dog- eared catalogue of facts and factors that have served their predecessors since at least the beginning of this century. At the level of analysis there is remarkably little to choose between, let us say, Latin America, its Rise and Progress, written in 1911 by F. Garcia Calderon and From Cortes to Castro published in 1974. Although a competent piece of work in terms of summarized information, Simon Collier's book lacks any guiding idea or hypothesis to provide some degree of coherence to its breathless narrative outline. As so often is the case with Englishmen nowadays, he appears both sensible and irresolute, especially when confronted with any choice involving enforced hardships. More concerned with the present than the past, Collier betrays little familiarity with the latest openings in historical research. However, whatever its defects, Collier's work is a model of industry and intelligence when compared to the text offered by Ronald Hilton which is presumably aimed at a popular audience of conservative persuasion. But what of the theory of Dependency? Here surely we will find our missing synthesis, or if you will, the new paradigm. Any such hope is soon shattered by closer acquaintance with the productions of this school. Eduardo Galeano proffers a sentimental catalogue of horrors, an unremitting account of capitalist exploitation across the centuries so bleakly determinist as to suggest that the continent indeed labours under some primal curse. Latin America, edited by Ronald Chilcote and Joel Edelstein, is a more serious work, consisting of a long, introduction in which the so-called Diffusionist model of development is contrasted unfavourably with the scheme of dependency, followed by equally long case-studies of Guatemala, Mexico, Argentina, Brazil, Chile and Cuba, each comprising a brief historical survey together with a more extended discussion of the political situation. It is immediately noticeable that the sanest pieces are written by Latin Americans. On Argentina, for example, Juan Corradi offers a relatively sensible analysis of the internal politics of his country. Moreover in the case of Theotonio dos Santos, one

His continued reliance on the under-consumptionist arguments so popular in the early 1960s is in large measure under-cut by his own admission that: ' Despite the abject poverty of fifty million inhabitants Brazil has another forty-two million who receive a reasonable income.' If this indeed be the case, then no matter how unjust the economic system may be, Brazilian industry has an ample market upon which to base its further expansion. On Mexico, James Cockcroft, who wrote so lively a book on the Flores Magon brothers and their group, proves strangely disappointing. The style is flaccid and the discussion oddly superficial. He writes: ' While the roots of Mexico's overall crisis go back to the Spanish Conquest, implementation of its contemporary developmentalist goal-structure derives mainly from the six-year presidency of Lazaro Cardenas.' He concludes with an exhortation for the Mexicans first to overthrow their government and then engage in battle against U.S. Imperialism. Needless to say, Donald Bray and Timothy Harding depict Cuba as the cynosure of the Americas. However, it is noticeable that whereas capitalist regimes are attacked for their failure to raise living standards, by contrast the Cuban government is praised for its avoidance of ' consumerism'. The new man of the socialist revolution will be impelled by moral rather than by material incentives. In sum, most of these essays are soft Marxist tracts, self-indulgent in their rhetoric, superficial or tendentious in their analysis, in which we can observe the once fertile hypotheses of the Dependency model already petrified into self-evident theorems, or best to say, dogmas of faith learnt and recited by rote. To write a study of the ' life and times ' of the Emperor Dom Pedro II is a daunt- ing task for any writer, but Professor Bernstein has some considerable experience in the field of Luso-Brazilian history and has had considerable success in the past in writing books specifically designed for undergraduate use. Dom Pedro II does, however, present any author with some formidable problems because not only did he rule Brazil for fifty years but, further, his personal impact upon the transition from colonial rule to independence left marks which can still be seen on many of the political and economic institutions of the country. The historian's task is not lightened by the fact that Pedro II managed rather than directed the course of political events between the attainment of his majority in 1840 and his overthrow in 1889. It is almost always more difficult to uncover the influences behind the execution of a policy than the influences which might dictate the simple enactment of a piece of legislation, and historians have still to examine the very extensive papers of the Emperor as well as those of the various institutions of the Empire in order to understand the way in which Pedro II' guided events ' through his use of patron- age.
